paragraphs: Comparing completed point clouds requires checking both the overall shape and how points represent local details. The paper argues that two common measures miss different aspects: Chamfer Distance can overlook local density differences, while Earth Mover’s Distance can emphasize the global distribution at the expense of detailed structure. Their unbounded scores also allow outliers to exert a strong influence.

The authors introduce Density-aware Chamfer Distance, derived from Chamfer Distance. It detects density mismatches, judges detailed structures more strictly than Earth Mover’s Distance, and is substantially cheaper to compute than that measure. Its bounded range is intended to make evaluation across a test set more stable.

In point cloud completion experiments, the proposed measure accounts for both global structure and local geometry, including cases where the existing measures disagree. Training with it also improves the same model’s results on all three measures compared with training using Chamfer Distance. A separate point discriminator guides down-sampling, improving the new score while remaining competitive on the older measures.
neurips-2021-balanced-chamfer-distance-a.tldr: Density-aware Chamfer Distance evaluates point cloud density and detail more comprehensively and also improves completion when used as a training loss.

paragraphs: Detecting an abrupt change can be difficult when only a few sensors carry useful evidence and monitoring every sensor is expensive. The paper studies a setting where a system chooses sensing actions sequentially and sees measurements only from those choices. It must therefore decide both where to look and when there is enough evidence to report a change.

The authors first derive an information-theoretic lower bound on detection delay for a general class of probability distributions described by finitely many parameters. This establishes a benchmark for what a detection method can achieve. They then design an efficient online strategy that balances trying different sensing options with repeatedly querying those that appear informative.

The proposed strategy comes with bounds on its expected detection delay. At low false alarm rates, these match the lower bounds, establishing optimality in that regime. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets also demonstrate effectiveness. The result connects adaptive sensor selection with a formal account of how quickly change can be detected under restricted observation.
neurips-2021-bandit-quickest-changepoint.tldr: An adaptive sensing strategy detects changes with delay bounds that match information-theoretic limits at low false alarm rates.

paragraphs: A multi-label classifier can assign several labels to one input, but it also needs a way to recognize inputs outside its familiar distribution. The paper addresses this less-explored uncertainty problem. Methods that rely on the largest label score discard information from the other labels, even though their combined behavior may help distinguish familiar inputs from unfamiliar ones.

The proposed method, JointEnergy, combines energy scores computed for individual labels into an overall indicator of whether an input is out of distribution. The authors also give this aggregation a mathematical interpretation through joint likelihood. This connects the combined score to information across labels rather than treating the most extreme individual score as sufficient.

Experiments on MS-COCO, PASCAL-VOC, and NUS-WIDE show consistent improvements over previous maximum-score approaches. The reported reduction in FPR95 reaches up to 10.05% relative to the previous best baseline. These findings support using information from multiple labels together for detection, with the largest reported improvement describing a best observed result rather than a uniform gain.
neurips-2021-can-multi-label-classificat.tldr: JointEnergy improves out-of-distribution detection for multi-label classifiers by combining energy scores across labels.

paragraphs: Generating a sharp video frame does not by itself solve the problem of predicting what will happen far into the future. The paper focuses on long-term dependencies in video: the relationships across time that a model must preserve to produce accurate extended predictions. Existing models can generate visually sharp images while still struggling with this longer horizon.

Clockwork VAE addresses the problem using a hierarchy of hidden sequences that update at different rates. Higher levels update less frequently, introducing temporal abstraction into the model. This gives the hierarchy distinct timescales for representing video content, instead of requiring every level to change at every step.

The authors evaluate the model on four diverse video prediction datasets with sequences reaching 1,000 frames and report that it outperforms leading video prediction models. They also introduce a Minecraft benchmark for long-term prediction. Additional experiments show that slower levels represent more slowly changing objects, while faster levels represent faster objects, supporting the intended role of the hierarchy.
neurips-2021-clockwork-variational-autoe.tldr: Clockwork VAE improves long-term video prediction using a hierarchy whose hidden representations update at different speeds.

paragraphs: Cross-view geo-localization identifies where a street-level photograph was taken by matching it to aerial images with known locations. The difficulty is that the same place can look dramatically different from the ground and from above. The paper introduces a layer-to-layer Transformer to capture broad visual relationships and reduce ambiguity between these views.

The model uses learned positional embeddings to help connect geometric arrangements across ground and aerial images. These embeddings are learned through the training objective, reducing reliance on the strong geometric assumptions used by some competing approaches. The authors also introduce self-cross attention, which connects adjacent layers rather than modeling relationships only within each layer.

These connections provide shorter routes for information to flow through the network. The paper reports more stable training, better generalization, and intermediate features that avoid becoming overly similar. Across standard, fine-grained, and cross-dataset evaluations, the model performs favorably against leading methods. Together, the findings support learning both spatial relationships and relationships between representation layers for this matching problem.
neurips-2021-cross-view-geo-localization.tldr: A Transformer with learned positional embeddings and attention across adjacent layers improves matching street photographs to aerial locations.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning methods are often compared using a single mean or median score across many tasks. Those summaries can conceal uncertainty from having only a few training runs. As benchmarks become more computationally demanding, small numbers of runs make it harder to tell whether apparent differences between algorithms support reliable conclusions.

The paper demonstrates this issue through an Atari 100k case study, where conclusions from point estimates differ substantially from those produced by fuller statistical analysis. It advocates reporting intervals around aggregate performance, using performance profiles to expose variability, and choosing more robust aggregate measures such as the interquartile mean.

The authors apply these tools to evaluations on the Arcade Learning Environment, Procgen, and the DeepMind Control Suite, again finding discrepancies in earlier comparisons. They provide the rliable library to support the proposed methodology. The contribution is an approach to making comparisons more trustworthy with a handful of runs, rather than treating a single aggregate score as a complete account of performance.
neurips-2021-deep-reinforcement-learning.tldr: Accounting for statistical uncertainty can change deep RL comparisons, motivating interval estimates, performance profiles, and robust aggregate scores.

paragraphs: Some performance measures, including AUC and F-measure, depend on collections of predictions rather than separate losses for individual examples. Directly training neural networks for these measures can involve solving a linear program inside training. The challenge is that its large constraint matrix depends on learned representations and changes as the network updates.

The paper develops a GPU-compatible approach using a generalized Newton method, drawing on ideas previously proposed for 1-norm support vector machines. The method requires little unrolling of the optimization procedure, improving efficiency when computing gradients backward through it. When the constraint matrix exceeds GPU memory, sufficient dimension reduction allows optimization in a smaller space while retaining accurate training gradients.

The resulting module applies across the described tasks without task-specific adjustments or relaxations. The authors study its properties and compare it with approaches based on surrogate lower bounds or specialized optimization procedures. They frequently observe better computational behavior and task performance, supporting direct optimization as a practical option for these coupled performance measures.
neurips-2021-differentiable-optimization.tldr: A differentiable linear-programming framework makes direct neural-network training for measures such as AUC and F-measure more practical.

paragraphs: Large language-processing models face deployment costs from both storage and inference computation. In BERT, much of that computation consists of matrix multiplications. The paper observes that ordinary matrix decomposition struggles to compress the weight matrices efficiently because they are not low-rank, even though the representations produced at each layer occupy a low-dimensional space.

DRONE uses this representation structure to construct a data-aware low-rank decomposition of the weights. The authors provide a provably optimal formulation with an efficiently computable closed-form solution. The method applies to both fully connected layers and self-attention layers, and it can further compress models that have already undergone distillation.

Experiments show smaller models and faster inference with limited accuracy loss. DRONE alone achieves a 1.92-fold speedup on MRPC with a reported 1.5% accuracy loss. Combined with distillation, it achieves more than 12.3-fold speedup on various natural language inference tasks. These results support using the structure of actual layer representations to guide compression.
neurips-2021-drone-data-aware-low-rank-c.tldr: DRONE compresses BERT using low-dimensional structure in layer representations, improving model size and inference speed with limited accuracy loss.

paragraphs: The paper studies two-player zero-sum games in which one player minimizes an objective and the other maximizes it. The minimizing problem may be nonconvex, while the maximizing objective must satisfy a Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition or strong concavity. Actions are continuous and unconstrained. The learning rule uses gradient descent and ascent operating on separated timescales.

Rather than asking only whether gradients become small, the authors examine whether learning reaches meaningful game-theoretic equilibria. They prove that every locally stable point of the corresponding continuous-time system is a strict local minmax equilibrium. This connects dynamical stability to a local equilibrium concept within the game classes studied.

Using timescale separation, a potential function, and a result about avoiding saddles asymptotically, the authors establish global asymptotic almost-sure convergence of the discrete updates to a set of strict local minmax equilibria. They also give rates for reaching approximate stationary points. Global convergence here concerns the learning process; the destination remains a local minmax equilibrium, not a claimed global optimum of an arbitrary game.
neurips-2021-global-convergence-to-local.tldr: For specified nonconvex zero-sum games, gradient descent-ascent with separated timescales converges almost surely and asymptotically to strict local minmax equilibria.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to keep learning without losing what it learned earlier. This paper considers the harder setting where task identities and boundaries are not supplied. A common approach stores a subset of past examples and replays them during training, but those unchanged examples may become less useful as the model evolves.

Gradient based Memory EDiting, or GMED, updates stored examples themselves using gradients in continuous input space. The edited examples remain similar to their originals while becoming more challenging for upcoming model updates. By anticipating examples that can incur higher loss, the method aims to make future replay more effective at countering forgetting.

GMED is designed to combine with other memory-based continual learning algorithms, making it a way to improve replay rather than a requirement to replace the surrounding learning method. Experiments support its effectiveness, with the strongest combined method significantly outperforming baselines and previous leading approaches on five of six datasets. The results suggest that maintaining a useful memory can involve adapting its contents over time.
neurips-2021-gradient-based-editing-of-m.tldr: GMED edits stored training examples to make replay more challenging and reduce forgetting during continual learning without task boundaries.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to generate music that follows the rhythm of human movement in a video. This requires identifying rhythmic structure in free body motion, including actions that do not already come with an obvious musical accompaniment. The proposed system, RhythmicNet, starts from skeleton keypoints extracted from the people moving in the video.

Its sequence of models builds a soundtrack in stages. First, frame-level body keypoints inform estimates of the musical beat and style pattern. A Transformer then generates drum instrument hits, while a U-net predicts their velocities and timing offsets. Further instruments are added by conditioning on the generated drum sounds, linking later musical content to the established rhythmic foundation.

The authors evaluate the system on large-scale video datasets containing movements with inherent sound associations, such as dance, and on internet videos showing varied movements and actions. They report plausible music that aligns well with different types of motion. The finding supports using explicit body movement as a basis for rhythmic soundtrack generation.
neurips-2021-how-does-it-sound-deb788cd3.tldr: RhythmicNet turns human body movements in video into musical soundtracks whose rhythms align with the motion.

paragraphs: A training algorithm influences more than how quickly a network fits its data: it also influences which solution the network reaches. The paper studies this implicit bias in diagonal linear networks. It analyzes stochastic gradient flow, a continuous-time version of stochastic gradient descent, to make the effect of randomness mathematically explicit.

The authors characterize the solution selected by the stochastic dynamics and prove that, in the setting studied, it has better generalization properties than the solution selected by ordinary gradient flow. They also show a surprising relationship between training speed and solution preference: slower convergence of the training loss produces a stronger beneficial bias.

The analysis includes convergence guarantees, and experiments support the theoretical claims. The central implication is that structured training noise can help select solutions with better generalization, rather than merely adding variability to optimization. Because the proof concerns diagonal linear networks and continuous-time dynamics, its contribution is a precise mechanism in that setting that helps explain advantages observed for stochastic gradient descent in practice.
neurips-2021-implicit-bias-of-sgd-for-di.tldr: For diagonal linear networks, stochastic gradient flow provably selects better-generalizing solutions than gradient flow, with stronger beneficial bias when training converges more slowly.

paragraphs: A learner can potentially learn more from an example when it understands why a cooperative teacher chose that example. The paper brings this idea from adaptive teaching into machine parameter learning. It asks how a student’s awareness of the teacher’s intention can improve learning beyond simply processing the examples presented.

The proposed iterative teacher-aware learner uses gradient-based optimization and incorporates the teacher’s cooperative intention into its likelihood function. This makes the teaching mechanism part of how the learner interprets information. The authors prove faster learning than the naive algorithms used in earlier machine teaching work and establish both local and global improvements for their iterative process.

Experiments examine regression, classification, and inverse reinforcement learning using synthetic and real data. The paper also reports benefits when agents learn from human teachers. Together, these results support treating cooperative example selection as useful information for parameter learning. The relevant comparison is with the naive learning approaches considered in the work, rather than an unrestricted claim about every possible teacher or learner.
neurips-2021-iterative-teacher-aware-lea.tldr: A learner that models its teacher’s cooperative intention can learn parameters provably faster than the naive approaches studied.

paragraphs: Predicting how a protein’s function changes when its sequence changes is important for understanding and designing proteins. The paper builds on the idea that evolution leaves information about function in patterns across protein sequences. Learning those patterns without functional labels can therefore provide a basis for predicting the effects of sequence variants.

Earlier approaches described in the paper fit a separate model to a family of related sequences. That makes each new prediction task require its own training process. The authors instead investigate whether protein language models can supply useful predictions directly, using zero-shot inference without additional training or supervision from experimental data.

They report state-of-the-art performance for capturing the functional effects of sequence variation under this zero-shot setup. The finding indicates that knowledge learned from protein sequences can transfer to variant-effect prediction without fitting a new model for each task. Here, zero-shot refers to how the trained language model is applied to the prediction task; the result does not describe a model that learned nothing beforehand.
neurips-2021-language-models-enable-zero.tldr: Protein language models achieve state-of-the-art mutation-effect prediction through zero-shot inference without additional training or experimental supervision.

paragraphs: Combining fMRI data from several sites introduces a problem: differences between measurements can reflect scanners, software, or the collection environment rather than biology. The paper studies how to reduce this site-specific variation when estimating hierarchical Sparsity Connectivity Patterns, or hSCPs. The aim is to obtain reproducible brain connectivity components while retaining biologically relevant differences.

The proposed method uses matrix factorization together with unsupervised adversarial learning. This combination targets unwanted variation associated with the collection site during component estimation. The distinction matters because removing variation indiscriminately would conflict with the goal of preserving meaningful biological patterns in the pooled data.

On simulated datasets, the authors report components with higher accuracy and reproducibility. On a multi-center clinical dataset, they show preservation of age-related variation. These findings address complementary parts of the objective: recovering consistent components and keeping a particular source of biological variation. The evidence supports reducing site effects in this estimation process without losing the age-related differences examined in the clinical data.
neurips-2021-learning-robust-hierarchica.tldr: Adversarial matrix factorization improves the reproducibility of hierarchical fMRI connectivity patterns while preserving observed age-related variation.

paragraphs: The paper studies online classification, where queries arrive one at a time and must immediately receive labels, even when an adversary chooses the queries. Its objective differs from counting wrong answers: it adds up the distances between queries and the regions associated with their assigned labels. This gives errors a geometric cost.

When the true labels come from a nearest-center partition in Euclidean space, the authors show that total loss can be bounded independently of the number of queries. Each point’s true label is determined by which of a fixed set of centers is closest. The guarantee therefore depends on a specific structure for the label regions.

The authors contrast this result with the difficulty of learning general convex sets, for which they establish an almost-linear loss lower bound. Their analysis builds on regret guarantees for contextual search and introduces a reduction from multiclass to binary classification. The results show how geometric structure can fundamentally change what is achievable under this distance-based online objective.
neurips-2021-margin-independent-online-m.tldr: Online classification under a nearest-center labeling rule can achieve total distance-based loss independent of the number of queries.

paragraphs: An interpolating regression model fits its training responses exactly, but different exact fits can generalize very differently. The paper asks which interpolator is optimal within a specified class: estimators linear in the response variable that may use the data, population covariance, signal-to-noise ratio, and prior signal covariance, but not the actual signal or training noise.

The authors derive a closed-form expression for this optimal interpolator. They also show that a particular initialization followed by preconditioned gradient descent approaches it in the limit. This links a statistical notion of optimality to the solution selected by an optimization procedure.

In one identified regime, the usual minimum-norm interpolator can generalize arbitrarily worse than their optimum. Numerical experiments further indicate that, with an isotropic prior, interpolating methods using only training data can achieve the proposed notion of optimality. The authors extend the framework to random features regression under a linear data-generating model. These results make the choice among exact fits central to understanding generalization.
neurips-2021-on-optimal-interpolation-in.tldr: The paper derives an optimal response-linear interpolator and identifies a regime where minimum-norm interpolation generalizes arbitrarily worse.

paragraphs: A neural network’s maximum expressive power does not tell us how complex its behavior will usually be. The paper studies this distinction for maxout networks, using the number of activation regions as a measure of complexity. Its focus is on how parameter choices distribute networks across functions of different complexity, rather than only on the most elaborate function an architecture can represent.

The authors show that practical complexity can fall far below theoretical maximum complexity, extending a phenomenon previously observed in deep ReLU networks. They also find this behavior when examining classification decision boundaries. In parameter space, many full-dimensional regions correspond to widely differing complexity levels, so this variation is not confined to isolated parameter choices.

The work also establishes nontrivial lower bounds on expected complexity, complementing the observation that maximum-based descriptions can be misleading. Finally, it investigates initialization procedures and shows that these can accelerate training convergence. Together, the findings connect representational complexity with the parameter choices that shape a network’s starting point and learning behavior.
neurips-2021-on-the-expected-complexity-.tldr: Maxout networks can have practical complexity far below their theoretical maximum, and initialization choices can speed training convergence.

paragraphs: The paper studies bandit optimization when the unknown reward function is non-concave, a setting less developed than linear or concave reward problems. Its examples include low-rank generalized linear bandits and bandits based on two-layer neural networks with polynomial activations. The central question is how learning requirements scale with the dimensions of these structured problems.

The authors develop a unified zeroth-order optimization framework and obtain dimension-optimal rates in several structured polynomial settings. For low-rank generalized linear bandits, their algorithm is minimax-optimal in its dimension dependence, refuting two earlier conjectures. They also apply the approach to reinforcement learning with a generative model, improving sample complexity over prior methods.

The analysis shows that standard optimistic approaches, including UCB, can be suboptimal by dimension factors. In the polynomial neural-network setting with noiseless rewards, the proposed algorithm uses a number of samples equal to the intrinsic algebraic dimension. Optimistic methods instead have worse dependence on the extrinsic dimension, with a gap that can be exponential in polynomial degree.
neurips-2021-optimal-gradient-based-algo.tldr: A unified optimization approach achieves dimension-optimal guarantees for several structured non-concave bandits and exposes dimension-dependent weaknesses of optimistic methods.

paragraphs: The paper examines distributed learning in which clients collaborate through a server while needing privacy from that server. Each round randomly selects a small fraction of data samples. Clients randomize their responses using local differential privacy, and the server receives a shuffled collection of responses without the association between each response and its client.

The authors develop a new analysis of Rényi differential privacy for this combination of subsampling and shuffling. Their principal result describes a tradeoff between privacy and optimization performance for discrete randomization mechanisms. The analysis also supports accounting for privacy across repeated rounds, which is central to iterative learning.

Numerical results show that, in important regimes, the composed bounds improve substantially over previous approximate differential privacy guarantees using strong composition. Experiments with real datasets also show better privacy-learning performance tradeoffs. The paper explicitly leaves a gap between its lower and upper privacy bounds unresolved, so the improved accounting does not settle the exact privacy limits of the analyzed setting.
neurips-2021-renyi-differential-privacy-.tldr: A new Rényi privacy analysis improves guarantees and privacy-learning tradeoffs for distributed learning that combines subsampling, local randomization, and shuffling.

paragraphs: Before a controller can optimize useful behavior, it may need to keep an unknown dynamical system stable. The paper addresses this foundational problem through direct policy search. It considers fully observed systems and develops a model-free algorithm, meaning the approach does not require first supplying an explicit model of the system’s dynamics.

The algorithm solves a sequence of discounted linear quadratic regulator problems while gradually increasing the discount factor. This staged procedure provides a route to a stabilizing controller without requiring an already stabilizing control policy as its starting point. Removing that prerequisite addresses a significant limitation of earlier work described in the paper.

The authors prove efficient recovery of a stabilizing controller for linear systems. For smooth nonlinear systems, the guarantee applies within a neighborhood of an equilibrium, giving a local stabilization result. Evaluations on common control benchmarks examine the method empirically. The contribution is both an algorithmic construction and a guarantee that policy-gradient methods can establish stability under the stated system conditions.
neurips-2021-stabilizing-dynamical-syste.tldr: A model-free policy-gradient method learns stabilizing controllers without an initial stabilizing policy, with guarantees for linear and locally smooth nonlinear systems.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning often assumes that labeled, unlabeled, and test examples come from the same distribution. The paper considers a broader requirement: a learner should classify familiar inputs while also recognizing inputs from an unknown distribution. This becomes especially challenging when labeled and in-distribution data are scarce and unfamiliar inputs may not appear during training.

The proposed approach, STEP, introduces a technique called Structure-Keep Unzipping. It learns a representation space in which out-of-distribution examples could be separated more effectively. This places the emphasis on how inputs are represented, so that detecting unfamiliar samples becomes easier in the learned space. The authors also derive an efficient algorithm for optimizing the objective.

Experiments across multiple out-of-distribution detection benchmarks show large improvements over the compared methods. These results support the effectiveness of the learned representation for the semi-supervised detection setting studied. The contribution directly addresses the combination of limited familiar data and potentially unseen unfamiliar examples, rather than relying on the usual assumption that all available data share one distribution.
neurips-2021-step-out-of-distribution-de.tldr: STEP learns representations that improve out-of-distribution detection when labeled in-distribution data are limited and unfamiliar samples may be absent during training.

paragraphs: In continuous control, an agent can sometimes benefit from continuing its previous action instead of choosing a different one at every step. TAAC incorporates this decision into an off-policy actor-critic algorithm. A second binary policy chooses between repeating the previous action and using a new action proposed by the actor.

The timing of this choice is central: the switching policy sees the action actually sampled by the actor before deciding whether to use it. This gives it more specific information than a decision based on the actor’s expected behavior. The method also provides persistent exploration and introduces a compare-through Q operator for multi-step value updates tailored to action repetition.

Across 14 continuous control tasks, TAAC demonstrates advantages over several strong baselines. The trained policies retain substantial action repetition while achieving top performance, even in tasks whose apparent structure seems unfavorable to repetition. This suggests that repeating actions can contribute to effective final behavior as well as helping an agent explore during learning.
neurips-2021-taac-temporally-abstract-ac.tldr: TAAC improves continuous control by learning when to repeat the previous action after inspecting a newly sampled alternative.

paragraphs: Auxiliary losses can encourage a neural network to follow useful assumptions about its inputs, but optimizing them only during training does not ensure the same behavior on new inputs. Adding them to the main training loss also changes the objective being optimized. The paper proposes a different way to incorporate these inductive biases.

Tailoring adapts a network after it receives an input and before it makes a prediction, using an unsupervised objective. This customizes the model to the current input without requiring its label. The authors then introduce meta-tailoring: a nested training procedure that judges task performance after the model has undergone this unsupervised adaptation.

This arrangement connects the adaptation step to the task objective the model ultimately needs to satisfy. Instead of merely asking a network to minimize an auxiliary loss during training, it trains for useful predictions following adaptation. The paper discusses theoretical advantages and demonstrates empirical benefits across diverse examples, supporting prediction-time optimization as a way to encode inductive biases.
neurips-2021-tailoring-encoding-inductiv.tldr: Tailoring adapts networks to each input using an unsupervised loss, while meta-tailoring trains them to perform well after that adaptation.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent learning must represent how joint behavior affects a shared outcome while remaining computationally manageable as agents are added. Value factorization addresses this tension by decomposing value functions. The paper develops a multi-agent fitted Q-iteration framework to analyze what such decompositions do and when the resulting learning process can converge.

For linear value factorization, the analysis reveals an implicit counterfactual credit-assignment mechanism. This helps explain how a simple decomposition can support reasoning about individual agents’ contributions to a collective result. However, the authors also show that the learning process may fail to converge in some settings.

Further analysis identifies two ways to improve convergence properties: on-policy training can help locally, while richer classes of joint value functions can help globally. The authors examine these theoretical implications empirically using illustrative examples and StarCraft II unit micromanagement tasks. The work therefore separates the usefulness of a decomposition for assigning credit from the conditions needed for reliable learning dynamics.
neurips-2021-towards-understanding-coope.tldr: Value factorization can implicitly assign credit among cooperating agents, but convergence depends on the training setup and joint value-function class.
